hook.situation: You talk about a teacher, parent, boss, or customer and need to show respect in the grammar itself.
objectives: Use -(으)시- to honor the sentence subject.
Use 께서 for a respected subject and 께 for a respected recipient.
Use special honorific verbs like 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다, and 드리다.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean honorifics are not just 'being polite'. 해요체 can be polite to the listener, but honorific grammar often honors the person you are talking about. 선생님께서 오세요 honors the teacher as the subject; 선생님께 말씀드려요 honors the teacher as the recipient.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)시- - subject honorific suffix
grammarNotes.mentalModel: -(으)시- raises the person who does or experiences the action.
grammarNotes.formation: Insert -(으)시- between the verb stem and the ending. Use -시- after a vowel or ㄹ stem: 오다 becomes 오세요, 살다 becomes 사세요. Use -으시- after a consonant stem: 읽다 becomes 읽으세요. Some verbs use special honorific forms: 있다 becomes 계시다, 먹다/마시다 becomes 드시다, 자다 becomes 주무시다, 말하다 becomes 말씀하시다.

examples.note: 오다 becomes 오세요 because the teacher is the honored subject.
계시다 is the honorific form of 있다 for people.
식사하시다 is a respectful meal verb.

examples.en: The boss is in a meeting now.
examples.note: 이다 becomes 이세요 when honoring the subject.

contrastPairs.explanation: Use -(으)시- for the respected subject, not for yourself.
계시다 is for respected people, not objects.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -(으)시- honors the subject. Do not use it on your own action just to sound polite.

exceptions: If the subject is a close friend or younger person, -(으)시- is usually unnecessary even in polite speech.
For some family members like 부모님, 할머니, 할아버지, honorific forms are normally expected.

grammarNotes.title: N께서 V-(으)시다 - respected subject
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 께서 marks who deserves respect as the subject of the sentence.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 께서 instead of 이/가 when the subject is someone you honor: 선생님께서, 어머니께서, 고객님께서. It often appears together with -(으)시- or a special honorific verb: 선생님께서 오셨어요, 어머니께서 말씀하셨어요.

b.en: I ask the teacher a question.

contrastPairs.explanation: 께서 marks the respected subject. 께 marks the respected recipient.
Both can be spoken Korean. 께서 is more explicitly respectful and formal.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 말씀하시다 honors the respected speaker. 말씀드리다 humbly describes your telling a respected recipient.

exceptions: 께서 can sound formal in casual speech. 이/가 with -(으)시- is often natural: 선생님이 오셨어요.
Do not use 께서 for non-human objects.

grammarNotes.title: N께 V-아/어 드리다 - respected recipient
grammarNotes.mentalModel: 드리다 lowers your action to respect the person receiving it.
grammarNotes.formation: Use 께 for the respected recipient and 드리다 for your action toward them: 부모님께 연락드려요, 선생님께 말씀드렸어요, 고객님께 안내해 드리겠습니다. This is not subject honorific; it is recipient honorific or humble speech.

examples.en: I will contact my parents first.

examples.note: The speaker humbly reports their action.

examples.en: I will guide the customer again.

contrastPairs.explanation: 말씀하시다 honors mother as speaker. 말씀드리다 humbly honors mother as recipient.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 부모님 are the recipient here, not the subject. Use 께, not 께서.

exceptions: 드리다 is not for everything. Use it when your action is directed toward someone respected.
For close friends, plain 주다 or 하다 is usually enough.

exampleSentence.ko: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
exampleSentence.en: When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
exampleSentence.note: The honored person can be the person being discussed.
The teacher is the respected subject.

exampleSentence.en: The boss is not here right now.
exampleSentence.note: Honorific form of 있다 for a respected person.
Honors the person eating or drinking.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give or do for a respected person

exampleSentence.note: Humbly describes your action toward a respected recipient.

exampleSentence.en: I will contact my parents first.
The boss is not here right now.
I will guide the customer again.

readingText.title: Who receives the respect?
readingText.body: 민서는 선생님에 대해 말할 때 높임말을 써요. 선생님이 주어일 때는 “선생님께서 오세요”라고 말해요. 선생님이 말하는 사람일 때는 “선생님께서 말씀하셨어요”라고 해요. 하지만 민서가 선생님에게 말한 일을 설명할 때는 “선생님께 말씀드렸어요”라고 해요. 께서는 주어를 높이고, 께는 받는 사람을 높여요. 그래서 높임말을 쓸 때는 먼저 누가 행동하는지, 그 행동이 누구에게 가는지 봐야 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo uses honorific language when talking about her teacher. When the teacher is the subject, she says, 'The teacher is coming.' When the teacher is the speaker, she says, 'The teacher spoke.' But when Minseo explains that she told something to the teacher, she says, 'I told the teacher.' 께서 honors the subject, and 께 honors the recipient. So when using honorifics, first check who is doing the action and who receives the action.

culturalNote.title: Respect has direction
culturalNote.body: Honorific Korean asks where respect is pointing. Sometimes it points to the subject with -(으)시- or 께서. Sometimes it points to the recipient with 께 and 드리다. Overusing honorifics on yourself sounds wrong, not extra polite.
culturalNote.tip: Before adding -시-, ask: who is the subject? Before using 드리다, ask: who receives my action?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence honors the teacher as subject?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께서 marks the respected subject, and 오세요 honors that subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence honors the teacher as recipient?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks the respected recipient, and 드리다 humbly describes your action.
계시다 is for respected people, not objects or yourself.
어머니 is the respected subject who spoke.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 제가 선생님께서 말씀드렸어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: The teacher is the recipient, so use 께, not 께서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 가방이 책상 위에 계세요.

bullets: 께서 marks a respected subject: 선생님께서 오세요.
께 marks a respected recipient: 선생님께 말씀드려요.
Special honorific verbs matter: 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다.
Do not use honorifics on yourself or on objects.
